questions.prompt: What is the core difference between a data migration and a metadata migration in a Salesforce project?
options: Metadata migration moves configuration (objects, fields, flows, code) via change sets or DX; data migration moves the business's actual record data, which has no equivalent automated deploy mechanism
Data migration only moves Apex code, while metadata migration moves everything else
There is no real difference — both terms describe the exact same activity
Metadata migration can only happen after a data migration is fully complete
Data migration is a feature built into Salesforce DX, while metadata migration requires a third-party tool
Metadata migration always requires Bulk API 2.0, while data migration never does
questions.explain: Metadata migration carries configuration between orgs with built-in, largely mechanical tools. Data migration carries the business's actual record data, which has no equivalent automated 'deploy' button and requires its own planning, design, and proving process.
questions.distractorExplain: Option C is wrong because the two are genuinely distinct problems with different tools and risks, not the same activity under two names — conflating them is exactly the mistake this course's first lesson warns against.

questions.prompt: An acquired company's contact phone numbers disagree between its old CRM and its support ticketing tool. Per this course's source-analysis practice, what should happen before migration design proceeds?
options: A deliberately decided system of record for that specific data has to be established, which may differ field-by-field or object-by-object rather than being the same source for everything
The two values should always be averaged or concatenated into one combined field
Whichever system was migrated from most recently automatically becomes authoritative
The field should be dropped from scope entirely rather than resolved
questions.explain: The system of record has to be deliberately decided, typically with input from people who actually use each source day to day, and it isn't necessarily the same system across every field or object — a different source can win for different data.

questions.prompt: Match each data-quality dimension to the problem it specifically measures, per this course's profiling lesson.
right: Whether a field's value conforms to its expected format or type
Whether required fields are actually populated
Whether related fields agree with each other across records or systems
How many records represent the same real-world entity more than once
questions.explain: Completeness checks whether required fields are populated. Uniqueness checks for duplicate representations of the same entity. Validity checks whether a value conforms to its expected format/type. Consistency checks whether related fields agree with each other — four independent dimensions that can each score differently on the same dataset.

questions.prompt: What is the main trade-off a project accepts by choosing a big-bang migration strategy instead of a phased one?
options: Big bang is simpler to plan with a single cutover, but concentrates all risk into one event and usually requires a longer freeze window
Big bang eliminates the need for any rollback plan, since nothing can go wrong in a single event
Big bang requires legacy and target systems to run side by side indefinitely
Big bang only works for migrations under 1,000 total records
questions.explain: Big bang is simpler to reason about — one migration, one cutover — but that simplicity comes from concentrating all risk into a single event and typically demanding a harder, longer freeze window than a phased approach would need for any one stage.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Bulk API 2.0 limits a single ingest job's data file to a maximum size of ________ MB.
questions.explain: Bulk API 2.0 caps a single ingest job's file size at 150 MB, with records beyond that needing to be split across multiple jobs — one of this course's verified, documented platform limits.

questions.prompt: A migration needs to load 2.3 million historical Case records (an object the Data Import Wizard doesn't support) as a one-time load. Which tool category does this course's four-question decision process point to?
options: Data Loader with Bulk API enabled, or Bulk API 2.0 directly, given the volume and the unsupported object
The Data Import Wizard, since it is the simplest tool to open
A manual copy-paste process directly into Salesforce Setup
No tool is capable of loading Case records under any circumstances
questions.explain: The Data Import Wizard doesn't support Cases and tops out well below this volume. Data Loader with Bulk API enabled (or Bulk API 2.0 directly) is built for exactly this combination of volume and unsupported-object requirements.

questions.prompt: What is a migration mapping document, as this course defines it?
options: The field-by-field record of exactly where every piece of source data goes in the target schema, including target API names, data types, and required-ness
A diagram showing which Salesforce users have access to which objects
The schedule showing when each cutover phase will occur
A list of every validation rule active in the target org
The Bulk API job Id and its per-record success/failure results
A record of which sandbox type was used for rehearsal
questions.explain: A mapping document is the field-by-field source-to-target record — source field, target field API name, data types, required-ness, and any transformation rule — that later design and validation work builds directly on top of.
questions.distractorExplain: Option E describes a Bulk API job's result set, which belongs to reconciliation (Chapter 3), not the mapping document built during design (Chapter 2) — the two are related but distinct artifacts serving different purposes.

questions.prompt: Splitting a legacy "Full Name" field into Salesforce's separate First Name and Last Name fields, using a documented business rule with edge-case fallbacks, is an example of which transformation category?
options: A derived/calculated field produced by a documented business rule
Cleansing
Standardization
Migration sequencing
questions.explain: This isn't a mechanical fix (cleansing) or a format change (standardization) — it computes two new values from one source field according to a business rule, which is exactly what a derived/calculated field transformation is.

questions.prompt: A migration includes Account, Contact, Opportunity, and a custom Service_Contract__c object with a master-detail relationship to Account and a lookup to Contact. Put these objects in the correct load order based on their dependencies.
questions.explain: Account has no in-scope dependencies and loads first. Contact depends on Account. Opportunity typically depends on Account (and often Contact). Service_Contract__c depends on both Account (master-detail) and Contact (lookup), so it has to load last, after everything it references already exists.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: an ________ field is a custom field flagged in its definition to store a record's identifier from the source system, enabling safe, re-runnable upsert loads.
questions.explain: An External ID field stores a record's legacy/source-system identifier. Marking it Unique and using upsert against it is what makes a migration load idempotent — safely re-runnable without creating duplicates.

questions.prompt: A team upserts Contacts against the Salesforce Id field instead of a true legacy External ID. What symptom does this course say to expect on a re-run of the same file?
options: The re-run creates an entirely new batch of duplicate records, since the file never contained a real Id to match against on the first run
The re-run silently does nothing at all, neither inserting nor updating
The re-run automatically converts to using the correct External ID
The re-run succeeds identically every time with no issues
questions.explain: Because the source file never actually contained a Salesforce Id at the time it was prepared, every re-run fails to find a match and inserts a fresh set of duplicates — the classic symptom of upserting against Id instead of a real External ID.

questions.prompt: Match each term from this course's files and audit-field lessons to what it actually is.
right: The legacy file-storage object linking directly to a parent record via ParentId
Connects a ContentDocument to the record(s) it's attached to in the modern Files model
Lets a migration insert set real historical values for CreatedDate and similar fields, generally only on insert
Salesforce's feature for tracking field-level changes over time, capped at 20 fields per object by default
questions.explain: ContentDocumentLink connects a ContentDocument to its parent record in the modern Files model. The Attachment object is the legacy equivalent, linking via ParentId. Field History Tracking tracks field-level changes, capped at 20 fields per object standard. The audit field override permission lets historical CreatedDate/LastModifiedDate values be set, but generally only at insert time.

questions.prompt: A legal team wants migrated Contract records to show their true original signing date in CreatedDate. What constraint does this course's audit-field lesson say applies to achieving that?
options: The real historical CreatedDate value has to be set at the moment the record is first inserted, since the override generally does not work on a later update
CreatedDate can be freely edited at any time after the record exists, with no restriction
This is impossible to achieve under any circumstances in Salesforce
It requires purchasing the Field Audit Trail add-on specifically
questions.explain: The audit-field override permission generally only works on insert, not on a later update — so a real historical CreatedDate has to be set at the moment of creation in the target org, which has a direct sequencing consequence for the load design.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about multi-level load validation, per this course's validation lesson.
options: A correct record count alone guarantees that every field mapped and loaded correctly
Referential integrity checks confirm relationship fields are actually populated and point at real records
Spot-checking a sample of records only proves those specific records are correct, not the whole load
Disabling validation rules during a load should be documented and explicitly reversed immediately afterward
Required-field completeness checks are unnecessary if the record count already matches
questions.explain: A correct record count says nothing about field-level correctness (a value in the wrong field can still produce a correct count), and completeness checks are a separate, necessary level — so the first and last statements are false. Referential integrity, the limits of spot-checking, and the discipline around re-enabling disabled validation rules are all accurate.

questions.prompt: Why does this course say Bulk API 2.0's per-record success/failure result set is directly useful for building a reconciliation report?
options: It gives the specific error reason for each rejected record, replacing the need to guess why records didn't load
It automatically fixes every rejected record without further action
It only reports a single pass/fail flag for the entire job, with no per-record detail
It is only available after the legacy system has been fully decommissioned
questions.explain: Bulk API 2.0 returns separate success and failure result sets with per-record status and, for failures, the specific error reason — exactly the raw material a reconciliation report needs instead of guessing at causes.

questions.prompt: Match each Salesforce sandbox type to its role in migration rehearsal, per this course's trial-migration lesson.
right: Complete copy of production, refreshed roughly every 29 days; the right target for a final, production-scale dress rehearsal
Metadata only, no production records; cannot meaningfully rehearse an actual data load
A template-defined subset of production data, refreshed roughly every 5 days; good for early, iterative rehearsals
questions.explain: Developer/Developer Pro carry no production data and can't rehearse a real load. Partial Copy holds a template-defined data subset with a fast refresh cycle, suited to early iteration. Full is a complete production copy with a slow refresh cycle, reserved for the final, most realistic dress rehearsal.

questions.prompt: Where should a cutover's freeze-window length actually come from, per this course's cutover lesson?
options: The actual load duration measured during rehearsal, with margin added
An estimate made before anyone has actually timed a real load
A fixed, universal duration applied identically to every migration project
Whatever duration the business prefers for scheduling convenience, regardless of load time
questions.explain: The freeze window has to be sized from the load duration actually measured during rehearsal, with margin, because duration frequently doesn't scale linearly from a smaller sample and an optimistic guess risks a freeze that's too short for the real load.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about rollback and the "point of no return," per this course's rollback lesson.
options: A rollback trigger should be a specific, measurable condition decided in advance, not a judgment call made during the cutover event
Restoring from a pre-cutover backup is cleanest when little else has changed in the target org since cutover
Hard Delete bypasses the Recycle Bin and requires its own "Bulk API Hard Delete" permission for a truly permanent rollback deletion
Rollback remains fully safe and available indefinitely, no matter how much new data users have created in the target org
The point of no return is defined as the moment the cutover runbook is written
questions.explain: A rollback trigger needs to be specific and pre-agreed; a backup restore is cleanest early, before much has changed; and Hard Delete's own permission matters when a rollback must be truly permanent. Rollback does NOT stay safe indefinitely — once users create new, unrelated data in the target org, a full rollback risks destroying it, which is exactly the 'point of no return' this lesson describes (not the moment the runbook is written).

questions.prompt: During hypercare, a user reports "my data is missing." What does this course's post-migration-support lesson say the realistic triage approach is?
options: Check the reconciliation report and mapping document first for that specific object/field, since most such reports turn out to be a mapping or scope gap rather than genuine data loss
Immediately initiate a full rollback of the entire migration
Assume the report is false and take no action at all
Permanently decommission the legacy system immediately to resolve the ambiguity
questions.explain: The large majority of 'missing data' reports trace back to a documented mapping or scope decision (an excluded field, a date cutoff, a restructured field) rather than genuine data loss — checking the documentation first is the disciplined response.

questions.prompt: In this course's Meridian Supply Co. case study, why was re-running the corrected Source B load (after building a cross-source de-duplication pass) described as "safe and fast"?
options: Because the team had used upsert against a real External ID from the first rehearsal attempt, making the load idempotent and safely re-runnable
Because the legacy Source B system had already been fully decommissioned by that point
Because Hard Delete had been used to remove every previously loaded record first
Because the Data Import Wizard replaced Data Loader for the corrected run
questions.explain: Because External IDs and upsert were used from the very first rehearsal attempt, re-running the load after fixing the de-duplication logic simply re-confirmed already-correct records and corrected the rest, without creating duplicates — the idempotent-load benefit from Lesson 9 paying off directly.
